native_result.query: How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?
native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB: Among Black respondents (race = "black") in this NLSY-1979 file - which contains no income variable, so economic level is operationalized as prior wealth (composite_wealth_1985) - incarceration (ever_jailed, jails 1985-1994) is associated with weaker wealth growth across 1985 -> 1990 -> 1996 at every prior-wealth level of Black men, and the dollar shortfall grows monotonically with prior wealth: about -$18k to -$34k at the low level (w1985 <= 0), -$24k to -$27k at the middle level ($0-$5,000) and -$44k to -$80k at the high level (> $5,000), a high-minus-low gradient of roughly -$57k (95% CI -$92k to -$22k), so that by 1996 jailed men held only about 16% of the mean wealth of comparable non-jailed Black men at the high level versus about 28-30% at the low and middle levels, with high-level jailed men losing wealth on average (-$6.1k) while their non-jailed peers gained +$70.4k. Matching on composite_wealth_1985 erases about 73% of the raw pooled gap (-$39.5k unmatched to -$10.8k matched) and only the high-wealth shortfall remains distinguishable from zero under strict 1:1 matching (-$45k, 95% CI -$77k to -$15k), so this is an association conditional on starting position - largely, though not entirely, reflecting that jailed men started lower, with a residual deficit concentrated where the most wealth was at stake - and not an estimate of what jail does to wealth on its own; in relative (percentile-rank) terms the deficit is similar at all three levels (about 11-19 percentile points) and the cross-level gradient is not statistically detectable (-0.064, 95% CI -0.162 to +0.036), so the gradient is one of dollar losses rather than of relative mobility, and the results for Black women (16 jailed of 1,548) are not conclusive.
native_result.WorkflowB: Executed analysis/nls_wealth_analysis.py (deterministic, verified identical across two runs). Data: data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv, 12,013 x 6 (race, sex, ever_jailed, composite_wealth_1985/1990/1996), no NaN; black = 3,013 (25.08%). No income variable exists (header search for income/earn/wage/salary/pay returns NONE), so 'income level' is operationalized as prior wealth composite_wealth_1985 under two definitions that coincide here (qcut tertile edges fall on the mass at zero): low <= 0, mid (0,5000], high > 5000. Principal sample race=='black' & sex=='male' (n=1,465; 143 jailed, 9.76%). For each level: mean and median wealth in 1985/1990/1996, change d85_96, DiD = mean(d85_96|jailed) - mean(d85_96|not jailed) with 2,000-replicate seeded percentile bootstrap CIs, plus median-based, percentile-rank and signed-log robust variants, and a bootstrap CI for the gradient DiD(high)-DiD(low). Selection addressed by matching on composite_wealth_1985 (the only available covariate): 1:1 nearest neighbour with $2,000 caliper with replacement, and a caliper-mean version (average of all controls within caliper) added because 1:1 matching degenerates in the low stratum (7 distinct controls, one carrying 88.9% of pairs). DiD before vs after matching quantifies the selection component (72.8% of the raw pooled gap). Sensitivity: S0 all rows, S1 excluding 1,715 rows with 0/0/0 wealth (14.3%, possible coded non-response), S2 dropping 1,899 exact duplicate rows, S3 both, S4 positive baseline wealth only; the hypothesis uses only what is consistent across variants. Also reported: full black cohort (both sexes) and black women (n=16 jailed, marked not conclusive). Explicitly ruled out in the workflow: inferring incarceration from place of residence ('Jail' as residence) is NOT APPLICABLE - the file has no residence/city/state/region/census/place column and ever_jailed is observed directly. Limitations kept visible: association only (no causal language, verified by regex), ever_jailed covers jails 1985-1994 with no post-1996 follow-up, duration or timing; 1990 temporally ambiguous; heavy right tail (max $4.06m) mitigated with medians/ranks; zeros possibly coded non-response; cohort aged ~20-30 in 1985 so low wealth is partly age-normative; wealth rounded to $100 in 81-90% of values.

sub_hypo.text: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
sub_hypo.context: Black individuals in the National Longitudinal Study of Youth's 1979 cohort.
sub_hypo.relations: Incarceration may have a smaller negative impact on wealth for the high-income group than for individuals at lower wealth ranges.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.

sub_hypo.text: Among Black men, incarceration is associated with weaker wealth growth from 1985 through 1990 to 1996 at every prior-wealth level, with a dollar shortfall that grows with prior wealth.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY-1979 respondents with race = black and sex = male (1,465 men, 143 jailed). Incarceration covers 1985–1994. No income variable exists, so economic level is defined by 1985 wealth: low <= $0, middle > $0 and <= $5,000, and high > $5,000.
sub_hypo.relations: Jailed men have weaker wealth growth than non-jailed men at all three starting-wealth levels. Dollar shortfalls are approximately $18k–$34k at the low level, $24k–$27k at the middle level, and $44k–$80k at the high level. The high-minus-low difference in jailed-versus-non-jailed mean wealth changes is approximately -$57k (95% CI -$92k to -$22k). This is an association, not a causal effect.

sub_hypo.text: By 1996, jailed Black men at the high prior-wealth level held about 16% of comparable non-jailed men's mean wealth, versus approximately 28–30% at the low and middle levels; high-level jailed men lost wealth while non-jailed peers gained wealth.
sub_hypo.context: Black male NLSY-1979 respondents, grouped by 1985 wealth: low <= $0, middle > $0 and <= $5,000, high > $5,000; jailed status refers to 1985–1994.
sub_hypo.relations: The jailed-to-non-jailed ratio of mean 1996 wealth is approximately 16% in the high stratum and 28–30% in the low and middle strata. Within the high stratum, mean 1985–1996 wealth change is -$6.1k for jailed men versus +$70.4k for non-jailed men.

sub_hypo.text: Matching Black men on starting wealth removes about 73% of the raw pooled wealth-growth gap associated with incarceration, but a statistically distinguishable shortfall remains in the high prior-wealth group under strict 1:1 matching.
sub_hypo.context: Black male NLSY-1979 respondents; matching uses only composite_wealth_1985. The workflow applies 1:1 nearest-neighbor matching with replacement and a $2,000 caliper, alongside a caliper-mean alternative because low-stratum 1:1 matching concentrates heavily on a few controls.
sub_hypo.relations: Matching reduces the pooled jailed-versus-non-jailed wealth-growth gap from -$39.5k to -$10.8k, a reduction of approximately 73%. Under strict 1:1 matching, only the high starting-wealth stratum (> $5,000) retains a shortfall distinguishable from zero: approximately -$45k (95% CI -$77k to -$15k). The association largely, but not entirely, reflects lower starting wealth among jailed men; it does not isolate a causal effect of incarceration.

sub_hypo.text: Among Black men, the incarceration-associated deficit in relative wealth mobility is similar across starting-wealth levels, with no statistically detectable cross-level gradient.
sub_hypo.context: Black male NLSY-1979 respondents, comparing 1985–1996 percentile-rank wealth mobility across low (<= $0), middle (> $0 and <= $5,000), and high (> $5,000) 1985 wealth levels.
sub_hypo.relations: Jailed men exhibit relative-mobility deficits of approximately 11–19 percentile points at all three levels. The high-minus-low gradient is -0.064 (95% CI -0.162 to +0.036), which is not statistically distinguishable from zero. The detectable starting-wealth gradient concerns dollar losses rather than relative mobility.

sub_hypo.text: The association between incarceration and wealth growth among Black women is inconclusive.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY-1979 respondents with race = black and sex = female: 1,548 women, including only 16 jailed during 1985–1994.
sub_hypo.relations: The analysis does not establish a conclusive relationship between incarceration and wealth growth for Black women.
